An independent re-verification pass against this document, done after the fact by re-deriving a
sample of claims directly from `git show HEAD:<path>` rather than trusting the original write-up.

**Accuracy — high.** ~12 sampled deltas across both platforms, all severities, "dramatic" and
"boring" claims alike, all matched the actual `HEAD` source exactly, including the ones most
likely to be overcalled:

- **WIN-001 / MAC-012** ("resolveSecurely inverts security") — confirmed verbatim on both
  platforms: `if IsDNSEncrypted() → plain UDP; else → DoH`. This is the single most damning
  finding in the document and it holds up exactly as stated.
- **MAC-042** (DNSSEC "presence-only") — confirmed; the function's own comment says "validate
  signatures" but the code only checks `!dnskeyRecords.isEmpty && !rrsigRecords.isEmpty`.
- **MAC-079/WIN-079** (non-constant-time HMAC compare), **WIN-115/MAC-115** (`default-key`
  literal), **WIN-076** (`EnableAutoDoh` misread), **MAC-070/103** (utun VPN heuristic),
  **WIN-092** (incomplete private-IP prefix list), **MAC-032** (`suffix(2)` parent-domain bug) —
  all confirmed verbatim, including exact line content.
- No fabricated API, no invented method name, no claim falsified in the sample.

**Baseline discipline — correct and load-bearing.** Pinning to `git HEAD` while the working tree
was under concurrent edits was the right call: `HEAD`'s `Windows/Syxx.Kit/DNSResolver.cs` still
has the fixed `0x1234` ID and no RCODE handling, while the working tree had already been partially
remediated by the time this audit ran. Reading the working tree instead would have produced
15-20 false positives.

**Severity calibration — plausible but top-heavy.** Distribution: S0 = 67 (29%), S1 = 114 (49%),
S2 = 43 (18%), S3 = 8 (3%) — 78% rated "major or worse." Every S0 sampled was individually
defensible (a verdict the user sees is provably wrong on realistic input), but the S0 tier does
double duty for both catastrophic verdict-flips and merely-serious crashes/hangs that arguably
belong at S1.

**Root-cause fan-out — the main structural caveat.** ~15-18 of the 232 line items are downstream
restatements of a small number of shared root causes, counted once per call site. "Empty/failed
comparison baseline renders as secure/clean" is its own delta in `VantageComparer`/`ContentWarp`
(the actual bug) **and again** in each of `SyxxCLI`, `SyxxMirror`, `SyxxWitness` on both platforms
— six-plus entries for what is functionally one fix at the library layer plus call sites that
inherit it for free. Similarly the compression-pointer-loop guard is flagged separately in
`DNSResolver` and in `DNSCapture`'s own duplicate copy of `parseName` on both platforms (4
entries) — legitimate, since the code really is duplicated, but still one *kind* of fix applied
four times. This isn't wrong — each entry describes a real, independently observable symptom at a
specific file:line, and no dedup was requested — but "232 deltas" should be read as **~35-45
independent root causes surfaced at ~232 call sites**, not 232 unrelated bugs. Worth keeping in
mind so remediation-cost estimates aren't linear in the delta count.

**Coverage gaps.** The Windows launcher's Option-A equivalent of the AAAA-only limitation
(MAC-095 on macOS) isn't separately called out for `Syxx/Program.cs`, even though the same
structure exists there — a minor omission, not an error. Also present in source but never given
its own delta: `LeakDetector.swift`'s default base domain is `leak.zzyn.net` while `SyxxCLI`'s
Option-B call site uses `leak.syxx.app` — a real, minor branding/domain-ownership inconsistency
that fell through the cracks between the per-file audits.

**Format — clean.** IDs are fully contiguous (MAC-001…116, WIN-001…116, no gaps or duplicates),
every entry follows the same `**ID** [Sx] file:~line — finding. **Impact:** ...` shape, and the
appendix preserving the original W/M table plus the concurrent agent's implementation notes was
the right call rather than silently destroying content `ROADMAP.md` still references.

**Bottom line.** This document held up under independent re-verification — no fabricated or
mischaracterized claim was found in the sample — and the HEAD-pinning methodology was
demonstrably necessary given the concurrent edits in flight. The main thing to keep in mind when
acting on this document: the 232-count has real per-line grounding but meaningful root-cause
fan-out (~35-45 distinct underlying defects), not 232 independent bugs.

# USER's identified deltas — design content (implemented)

Deltas listed here are top priority.

## 1. Unified DNS Synthesis Engine: System Design & Research

This design introduces a client-side, offline, deterministic synthesis engine (`SyxxSynthesisEngine`) in `SyxxKit`/`Syxx.Kit`. It aggregates raw datapoints from the six canonical disciplines into a unified verdict with mathematically modeled confidence and probability scores, falling back to community review when findings are ambiguous.

---

### Part A: Individual Datapoint Evidence Reference

| Canonical Discipline | Collected Datapoint | Standalone Security Verdict / Implication | Risk Tier |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `RCODE == REFUSED / SERVFAIL` | Policy-based resolver censorship, DNS blocking, or severe resolver misconfiguration. | Medium |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `RCODE == NXDOMAIN` | Sinkholing (policy blocking), domain retirement, or typo redirection. | Low-Med |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `Transaction ID Mismatch` | Active on-path DNS spoofing attempt or race condition; injector raced the real resolver. | High |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `QR == 0` in response payload | Spoofing attempt / query injection accepted as a response by primitive parsers. | High |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `DNSSECStatus == signatureExpiredOrNotYetValid` | Replay attack (serving outdated records to bypass revocation) or client clock drift. | Medium |
| **1. Prophet** (Resolution) | `DNSSECStatus == unsigned` | Unsigned zone, or active DNSSEC stripping attack by on-path interceptor. | Low-Med |
| **2. Mirror** (Tampering) | `ComparisonResult.isRedirectionDetected == true` | Definite DNS hijacking, cache poisoning, or local split-horizon DNS routing. | High |
| **2. Mirror** (Tampering) | `ContentWarp.localHTML` vs `remoteHTML` hash mismatch | Content injection, transparent HTTP proxy caching, or block-page redirection. | High |
| **2. Mirror** (Tampering) | `ContentWarp.responseCode` in [403, 451, 302, 307] | HTTP-level censorship, legal blocking, or captive portal redirection. | High |
| **3. Portal** (Diagnostics) | Resolver IP belongs to unrecognized local MAC | LAN rogue resolver (rogue DHCP server, gateway takeover, or ARP spoofing). | High |
| **3. Portal** (Diagnostics) | `CaptivePortalStatus == yes` | Captive portal active; all outbound HTTP/DNS traffic intercepted and redirected. | Medium |
| **3. Portal** (Diagnostics) | `EncryptedDNSStatus == no` | Unencrypted transport; DNS queries sent over UDP/53 are subject to passive sniffing. | Medium |
| **3. Portal** (Diagnostics) | Resolver IP on loopback (`127.0.0.1` / `::1`) | Local proxy (AdGuard, NextDNS CLI) intercepting local traffic; upstream is unverified. | Low |
| **3. Portal** (Diagnostics) | Traceroute last-responding hop is private IP | ISP/Network transparent redirection or routing loop inside the local ISP gateway. | Medium |
| **4. Glutton** (Leak Detect) | `LeakVerdict == confirmed` | VPN DNS Leak; queries bypassed the tunnel, exposing user traffic to physical ISP. | High |
| **5. Cage** (Capture/Forens) | Subdomain Shannon Entropy $\ge 3.8$ bits/char | Potential DNS tunneling (exfiltration, command & control, or VPN-over-DNS). | High |
| **5. Cage** (Capture/Forens) | Inter-arrival Coefficient of Variation (CV) $< 0.2$ | Automated machine beaconing (botnet C2 heartbeat or telemetry) instead of human. | Medium |
| **5. Cage** (Capture/Forens) | Process initiator is `unsigned / AdHoc` | Unauthorized local code executing DNS lookups (untrusted executable or script). | Medium |
| **6. Witness** (Identity) | Sentinel config change (resolver added) | Unauthorized change to local network config (malware or rogue DHCP lease). | High |

---

### Part B: Cross-Discipline Relational Synthesis

Individual probes are informative, but their relationships provide conclusive proof of specific network states:

1. **DNSSEC Stripping + Tampering**:
   - *Formula*: `isRedirectionDetected == true` **AND** `DNSSECStatus == unsigned` (when public vages show valid signatures).
   - *Meaning*: The attacker hijacked the IP resolution and stripped out the DNSSEC security records to prevent validation errors.
2. **Local Captive Portal Interception**:
   - *Formula*: `CaptivePortalStatus == yes` **AND** `isRedirectionDetected == true` **AND** `ContentWarp.responseCode != 200`.
   - *Meaning*: Disregard "tampering" alerts; the client is in a local captive portal redirect loop.
3. **ISP Transparent Proxying (Silent Hijacking)**:
   - *Formula*: `isRedirectionDetected == false` **AND** `EncryptedDNSStatus == no` **AND** `LeakVerdict == confirmed` **AND** Observed Resolver IPs in collector match none of the configured system DNS servers.
   - *Meaning*: The ISP is silently intercepting UDP/53 queries at the network edge and routing them through their own resolvers, regardless of client configuration.
4. **Malicious C2 over DNS Tunnel**:
   - *Formula*: `Shannon Entropy >= 3.8` **AND** `Beacon CV < 0.2` **AND** Process Initiator is `unsigned / AdHoc` and resides in `/tmp` or `~/Downloads`.
   - *Meaning*: High confidence malware DNS exfiltration/command and control.
5. **Rogue Local Resolver Takeover**:
   - *Formula*: Configured DNS server matches a MAC address from LAN cartography that was not previously registered, and traceroute to a public IP terminates at that same hop.
   - *Meaning*: Direct DHCP/ARP redirection to an rogue machine on the local network segment.

---

### Part C: Verdict Logic & Scoring Engine

The synthesis engine evaluates 7 Candidate Conclusions:

1. `SECURE_CLEAN` (No anomalies)
2. `ACTIVE_TAMPERING_HIJACKING` (DNS poisoning or MITM)
3. `VPN_DNS_LEAK` (VPN bypass)
4. `LAN_ROGUE_RESOLVER` (DHCP/ARP hijacking)
5. `SUSPICIOUS_EXFILTRATION` (Tunneling/C2)
6. `CAPTIVE_PORTAL_INTERCEPT` (Hotspot captive redirect)
7. `INCONCLUSIVE_DEGRADED` (Insufficient data, timeouts, or network down)

#### 1. Credibility Score Calculation (Weight Rules)

Each conclusion starts with a base score of $0$ and accumulates points based on conditions:

```swift
// Pseudo-logic for credibility point accumulation:
var scores = [Conclusion: Double]()

// ACTIVE_TAMPERING_HIJACKING
if isRedirectionDetected { scores[.tampering, default: 0] += 50 }
if contentHashMismatch { scores[.tampering, default: 0] += 30 }
if transactionIdMismatch || qrBitZeroInResponse { scores[.tampering, default: 0] += 40 }
if dnssecStrippingDetected { scores[.tampering, default: 0] += 20 }

// VPN_DNS_LEAK
if vpnActive && leakVerdict == .confirmed { scores[.vpnLeak, default: 0] += 95 }
if !vpnActive && leakVerdict == .confirmed { scores[.vpnLeak, default: 0] += 20 }

// LAN_ROGUE_RESOLVER
if resolverMatchesUnrecognizedLanDevice { scores[.rogueResolver, default: 0] += 80 }
if arpSpoofingDetected { scores[.rogueResolver, default: 0] += 50 }

// SUSPICIOUS_EXFILTRATION
if highEntropySubdomains { scores[.exfil, default: 0] += 30 }
if beaconingRegularCadence { scores[.exfil, default: 0] += 30 }
if processIsUnsigned { scores[.exfil, default: 0] += 40 }

// CAPTIVE_PORTAL_INTERCEPT
if captivePortalDetected { scores[.captivePortal, default: 0] += 90 }

// SECURE_CLEAN
if !isRedirectionDetected && !contentHashMismatch && leakVerdict != .confirmed && !highEntropySubdomains && !processIsUnsigned {
    scores[.secure, default: 0] += 100
}
```

#### 2. Normalization & Probability Calculation

To derive the probability score for each conclusion:
$$\text{Probability}(C_i) = \frac{\text{Score}(C_i)}{\sum_{j} \text{Score}(C_j)} \times 100\%$$
*(If all scores are 0, probability is distributed 100% to `INCONCLUSIVE_DEGRADED`).*

#### 3. Confidence Score calculation

The Confidence Score (0-100%) represents the completeness and reliability of the evidence. It starts at $100\%$ and gets penalized for missing or degraded probes:

- Any vantage point query timeout: **-15%**
- Captive portal active: **-30%** (captive portals distort all internet probes)
- No internet connection / DNS queries fail entirely: **-80%**
- Collector leak check inconclusive: **-15%**
- Process attribution lookup fails (process unknown): **-10%**

---

### Part D: Reddit Fallback & Report Generator

When either condition is met:

1. **Confidence Score is less than 75%**
2. **The top probability score does not exceed the second-most likely by at least 30 points (30%)**

The client automatically flags the result as **Ambiguous** and provides the Reddit fallback flow:

#### 1. Clip-to-Clipboard Reddit Payload Format

```markdown
*** SYXX OFF-LINE ANALYSIS EVIDENCE REPORT ***
Generated: [12-Hour ISO Timestamp]
OS Version: [macOS Mojave+ / Windows 11]

[CONCLUSION SUMMARY]
⚠️ Result: AMBIGUOUS (Referral to Community Experts)
- Top Conclusion: [Conclusion Name] ([Probability]%)
- Second-Most Likely: [Conclusion Name] ([Probability]%)
- Synthesis Confidence Score: [Confidence]%

[DATA AND STATISTICS]
- Configured Resolvers: [Resolver list]
- VPN Tunnel Present: [Yes/No] (Interface: [Name])
- Captive Portal: [Yes/No/Unknown]
- Vantage Comparer Status: [Secure/Tampered/Degraded/Inconclusive]
- Local vs Public IP Sets: Local: [IPs] | Public: [IPs]
- Content Warp Status: [Body Hash Match/Mismatch] (HTTP Status: [Code])
- Leak Test Verdict: [Confirmed/NotDetected/Inconclusive]
- LAN Cartography: [Devices count] active MACs | Resolver MAC: [MAC/IP]
- Capture Metrics: [Total Packets], [Entropy Score], [Max Beacon CV]

[DNS CAPTURE LOG SAMPLE]
[First 10 lines of captured queries]
[Time] [Dir] [Domain] -> [Rcode] [Process Name]

[RECOMMENDED ACTION]

Experienced network security analysts can inspect the raw data to determine
if active hijacking, split-horizon routing, or portal redirects are at play.
```

### Part E: Implementation Class Blueprint

Below is the design contract to implement in `SyxxKit` and `Syxx.Kit`:

```swift
public struct SynthesisResult: Codable, Sendable {
    public enum Conclusion: String, Codable, Sendable {
        case secureClean = "Secure (Clean)"
        case activeTampering = "Active Tampering / Hijacking"
        case vpnDnsLeak = "VPN DNS Privacy Leak"
        case lanRogueResolver = "Rogue Local Resolver Takeover"
        case suspiciousExfil = "Suspicious DNS Exfiltration/C2"
        case captivePortal = "Captive Portal Redirect"
        case inconclusive = "Inconclusive / Degraded Evidence"
    }

    public let primaryConclusion: Conclusion
    public let confidenceScore: Int
    public let probabilities: [Conclusion: Int]
    public let explanation: String
    public let requiresRedditReferral: Bool
    public let nextSteps: [String]
}

public final class SyxxSynthesisEngine {
    public static func synthesize(
        prophet: DNSResponse?,
        dnssec: DNSSECStatus,
        mirror: ComparisonResult?,
        warp: WarpResult?,
        network: NetworkStateReport,
        leak: LeakTestResult?,
        forensics: ForensicsReport?,
        sentinel: SentinelDiff?
    ) -> SynthesisResult {
        // Deterministic weights, normalization, and referral calculations
    }
}
```

### Part F: Next Steps and Recommendations for the End User

- **For `ACTIVE_TAMPERING_HIJACKING`**:
  1. Immediately enable encrypted DNS profiles (DoH/DoT) using trusted public providers (Cloudflare `1.1.1.1` or Google `8.8.8.8`).
  2. Avoid inputting passwords or credentials on sites that return SSL/TLS certificate warnings.
- **For `VPN_DNS_LEAK`**:
  1. Toggle your VPN client's "Kill Switch" or "Block non-VPN traffic" setting.
  2. Disable IPv6 stack in your OS network settings if the VPN is IPv4-only.
- **For `LAN_ROGUE_RESOLVER`**:
  1. Disconnect from the local Wi-Fi or Ethernet link.
  2. Log in to your router gateway and verify that DHCP DNS options have not been modified.
- **For `SUSPICIOUS_EXFILTRATION`**:
  1. Run a system-wide antivirus or malware check.
  2. Locate the reported PID/process path and quarantine the untrusted executable.

### Evaluation & Peer-Review Remarks (2026-07-06)

This system design details a deterministic, client-side offline synthesis engine. Below is the vetting evaluation of the proposal:

#### 1. Core Strengths & Efficacy

- **Explainability & Trust**: By using pure weighted logic instead of machine learning, the engine ensures that every conclusion is fully explainable, trace-backed, and signable by the `WitnessSigner` evidence layer. This conforms exactly to the project's core values.
- **Ambiguity Containment**: The triggers for Reddit fallback (confidence $< 75\%$ or margin between top-two hypotheses $< 30$ points) are well-calibrated to contain false-secure conclusions, shifting the civil liability of edge cases to community experts.
- **Relational Synthesis**: The cross-discipline rules (such as captive portal detection modifying/dampening tampering alerts) are highly logical and prevent false positives on commercial public networks.

#### 2. Technical Gaps & Refinement Areas
>
- > [!WARNING]
  > **HTTP Status Classifications**: Part A marks HTTP statuses `[302, 307]` as High Risk tampering. Standard web redirects are common and benign. Treat standard redirects as inconclusive context modifiers; restrict High Risk verdicts only to explicit block pages (e.g., HTTP `451` or captive redirects on non-captive networks).
- > [!TIP]
  > **Confidence Math**: Calculating confidence via simple subtraction (e.g., $-80\%$ for offline, $-30\%$ for captive portal) can produce negative confidence scores. Restructure the engine to use multiplicative penalties:
  > $$\text{Confidence} = 100 \times \prod_{i} (1 - \text{Penalty}_i)$$
  > This bounds confidence strictly between $0$ and $100$ and models compounding uncertainty naturally.
- **Signer Blindspot**: The exfiltration detection rule (Part B, Rule 4) heavily weights `unsigned / AdHoc` processes. Attackers can execute DNS exfiltration via signed utilities (e.g., standard web browsers, system-signed command-line tools, or DLL sideloading). The engine should evaluate domain entropy and beacon cadence independently of signing status, using the signature as a secondary modifier.

#### 3. Recommended Canary Probes

To resolve the most common source of ambiguity (is this NXDOMAIN a block or a true non-existent domain?), the implementation should include two canaries:

1. **NXDOMAIN canary**: Query a random nonexistent UUID hostname. A non-NXDOMAIN response indicates active DNS hijacking.
2. **DNSSEC control canary**: Query a known-good DNSSEC-signed domain (e.g., `sigok.dane.verisignlabs.com`). A bogus verification indicates active DNSSEC signature stripping.

*Vetting status:* Approved. Ready to slate for implementation.

---

### Perplexity's comments**

Your synthesis engine is directionally strong: it is explainable, deterministic, and well-suited to offline client-side verdicting. The main refinements are to soften standard HTTP redirects, make confidence multiplicative, and treat process signing as a modifier rather than a gate for exfiltration detection.

#### What to keep

The cross-discipline approach is the right design choice because DNS hijacking, captive portals, DNSSEC downgrade/stripping, and tunneling often require correlating several weak signals rather than trusting one probe alone. High-entropy subdomains and regular beacon cadence are established indicators of DNS tunneling or C2-style activity, so those features belong in the core scoring model.

#### What to change

Standard `302` and `307` redirects are common and can be benign, especially in captive portal flows, so they should not automatically imply high-risk tampering without supporting evidence like a block page or portal context. A better confidence model is multiplicative, because it keeps the score bounded and reflects compounding uncertainty more naturally than repeated subtraction. Also, DNSSEC stripping and hijacking should be inferred from validation failures and control-canary behavior, not from an `unsigned` result alone, since unsigned or non-validating paths can occur for benign reasons too.

#### Practical canaries

A random NXDOMAIN canary is useful because an unexpected non-NXDOMAIN answer can expose resolver manipulation or interception. A known DNSSEC-signed control domain is also a solid validation probe, because it helps distinguish real DNSSEC failure from ordinary NXDOMAIN or local misconfiguration.

#### Suggested rule updates

- Treat `302` and `307` as portal-context signals, not high-risk tampering by themselves.
- Keep `451` and explicit block-page evidence as stronger tampering indicators.
- Evaluate entropy and beaconing independently of code signing, then use signing status as a confidence booster or reducer.
- Prefer canary-based confirmation for DNS hijacking and DNSSEC stripping rather than relying on a single anomalous response.

#### One implementation note

Your fallback threshold is sensible, but it will be more robust if "ambiguous" is triggered by both low confidence and weak separation between the top hypotheses, because captive portals and transparent proxies can otherwise mimic hijacking patterns.

Use a two-layer approach: first classify the network state from probe behavior, then dampen or boost confidence with a multiplicative model so one degraded signal cannot dominate the verdict. For DNSSEC stripping, the strongest pattern is a failure on a known-good signed control domain while the same resolver still answers ordinary queries, because DNSSEC is specifically designed to detect altered-in-transit answers through its RRSIG/DNSKEY/DS chain of trust.

#### Captive portal vs proxy

A captive portal usually shows redirect behavior tied to access control, often after the device checks for internet reachability; DNS redirection and HTTP 302-based login flows are common portal techniques. Transparent proxies are different because they sit inline and forward traffic silently, so you usually need endpoint, header, timing, or destination-behavior clues rather than a single redirect event to tell them apart. In practice, if DNS is redirected and an HTTP test page consistently lands on a login or terms page, that looks more like captive portal behavior; if ordinary browsing is altered without a portal login step, treat it as proxy/interception context and not automatically as tampering.

#### Multiplicative confidence

A clean implementation is to start at 100 and multiply by $$(1 - penalty)$$ for each degraded probe class, with each penalty capped in a reasonable range so confidence never goes negative. Example: if timeout penalty is 0.15, captive-portal penalty is 0.30, and process attribution penalty is 0.10, then confidence becomes $$100 \times 0.85 \times 0.70 \times 0.90 = 53.55$$, which is a much safer representation of partial evidence than subtracting fixed points. This works well because DNSSEC failure, leak checks, and portal interference are not independent in the real world, so compounding uncertainty is more realistic than linear deduction.

#### DNSSEC canaries

For a control canary, use a known DNSSEC-signed domain and verify that the validating path returns the expected result; if the domain resolves but validation fails, that is strong evidence of stripping or downgrade behavior. For a random NXDOMAIN canary, generate high-entropy, never-reused names and expect NXDOMAIN from the authoritative path; unexpected positive answers, rewrites, or consistent alternate IPs can indicate hijacking or search-domain pollution. Keep canaries short-lived, randomized per session, and segregated from user-visible domains so a cached or learned response cannot falsely train the resolver into a stable-but-wrong answer.

#### NXDOMAIN canary hygiene

Treat random NXDOMAIN canaries as disposable probes, not persistent indicators, because repeated use can create noise and may be confused with typo traffic, startup lookups, or local application behavior. Log the queried label, resolver used, and response code, but avoid reusing the same canary name across runs, since stable names can be cached or recognized by intermediate systems. If the NXDOMAIN canary returns anything other than a true negative from the expected path, escalate only when it co-occurs with other signals such as redirect detection, DNSSEC validation failure, or mismatch between configured and observed resolvers.

#### Exfiltration scoring

Do not require unsigned or AdHoc process status for exfiltration suspicion, because signed tools and browsers can still tunnel data over DNS. Instead, score high-entropy labels, long labels, and regular beacon cadence independently, then use process provenance as a secondary multiplier: unsigned processes increase confidence, but signed processes do not clear the alert if the network pattern is strong. That avoids over-triggering on legitimate signed software while still catching real DNS C2 behavior that manifests as repeated, structured lookups.

#### Suggested rule shape

- Captive portal: portal-specific redirect behavior plus login/terms page evidence, with DNS redirection treated as context rather than proof by itself.
- Transparent proxy: altered browsing behavior without a portal-login flow, ideally confirmed by response-path or destination inconsistencies rather than a single 302.
- DNSSEC stripping: signed control canary fails validation while ordinary DNS still works, especially if the resolver path is otherwise stable.
- NXDOMAIN canary: random label, one-shot use, and only strong when paired with other anomalies.
- Exfiltration: entropy + cadence first, signing status second.

### Claude's evaluation (2026-07-06) — Perplexity's points + reconciliation with DoW #3

**Concur with Perplexity; adopt all three core refinements — and they resolve the two open questions I left on DoW #1.**

1. **302/307 as context, not tampering — adopt.** Bare 3xx belongs in the Mirror/Warp *evidence
   adapter* as a portal/interception *context modifier*, never a High verdict. Reserve strong tamper
   weight for HTTP 451, a matched block-page fingerprint, or an SRI/TLS failure. Disambiguation
   (also Perplexity): 3xx → login/terms page = captive portal (dampens spoofing/interception);
   3xx that alters ordinary browsing with no portal login = interception *context* (weak signal only).

2. **Multiplicative confidence — adopt; it settles my DoW #1 peer-review Q(a)/Q(b).** The clean model
   is *two orthogonal axes*, which reconciles his math with my softmax rather than replacing it:
   - **Probability `P(Hᵢ)`** — softmax over accumulated log-weights → *which* hypothesis.
   - **Confidence** — `100 × ∏(1 − penaltyᵢ)` over degraded/missing/uncertain signal classes → *how
     sure*; bounded [0,100], never negative (fixes the subtraction bug the Parts-A eval flagged).
   - Referral trigger unchanged: confidence < 75 **or** top−second margin < 30.
   - Q(a) resolved: keep H4 content-tampering in v1, but it fires only on block-page/SRI/TLS evidence.

3. **Signing as a modifier, not a gate, for exfil — adopt; this is also a code delta.**
   `ExfilAnalyzer.assess` must score entropy + label length + beacon cadence *independently*, then
   apply signing as a secondary multiplier (unsigned boosts; signed does **not** clear). **Action:**
   verify the shipped `ExfilAnalyzer`/`ExfilAssessment` doesn't gate suspicion on `unsigned/AdHoc`;
   file a delta if it does. → **Verified 2026-07-06:** `ExfilAnalyzer.assess()` scores
   `highEntropy && regular → likelyExfil` on entropy + beacon cadence + blocklist only; process
   signing never enters (it lives in the separate capture/attribution layer). No delta needed; the
   Cage adapter consumes this signing-independent `suspicion`.

4. **Canary hygiene — adopt; it changes the evidence weights.** Both canaries are one-shot, per-session,
   high-entropy, segregated probes, and — critically — **weak on their own**: an anomalous canary only
   escalates when it co-occurs with another signal (redirect, DNSSEC-fail, or configured-vs-observed
   resolver mismatch). In the weight table, `canary_anomaly` gets a low base weight and a large
   *corroboration* bonus, not a standalone verdict. DNSSEC control: query a known-good signed name and
   validate the chain *ourselves* via `DNSSECVerifier` (stripping happens between us and the
   authoritative, so stub-side validation is the whole point); add a complementary known-bogus
   `sigfail`-style canary to tell "resolver validates" from "path strips."

**The point the review doesn't reach — and it's the important one: reconcile with DoW #3's vocabulary.**
Multiplicative confidence elegantly handles **Degraded**, but DoW #3 correctly separates **Untested**
and **Invalidated** as *hard* states that must **not** be folded into a probability or a confidence
penalty. A section that never ran (Untested) or whose premise failed (Invalidated — e.g. CID-001's
`8.8.8.8` substitution, CID-002's records-only status loss) contributes **no evidence** and must be
surfaced as its own label, not diluted into "61% confident." So the accumulator needs a **status
pre-pass**:

  1. Classify each of the six sections: `untested | invalidated | inconclusive | degraded | ran(finding)`.
  2. Only `ran`/`degraded` sections feed the softmax; `degraded` sections additionally contribute a
     confidence penalty (Perplexity's `1−penalty`).
  3. `untested`/`invalidated` sections never contribute a hypothesis weight; they **cap** the overall
     (cannot reach `clean` while a required section is untested) and are listed explicitly.

**Consequence for the contract already landed (`Synthesis/Conclusion.{swift,cs}`, both platforms):**
`Conclusion` currently exposes only `Hypothesis.inconclusive`, which is too coarse for DoW #3. It needs
a per-section **`SectionStatus`** axis (`untested/invalidated/inconclusive/degraded/ran`) and the
overall must respect it (never print `clean` with an untested required section). The change is
*additive* (a new enum + a `[Section: SectionStatus]` field), so Antigravity's mock still builds. I'll
amend the contract + `GUI_HANDOFF.md` on the go-ahead.

**Net:** the round has converged. Reconciled combiner =
*status pre-pass (DoW #3) → softmax probabilities → multiplicative confidence (Perplexity) →
margin/confidence referral*. I'll hold combiner implementation until this reconciliation is
acknowledged (it changes the contract), but the **two canaries are unaffected** and can proceed now
with the corroboration-weighted design above.

## Current working-tree re-audit — 2026-07-04 [done]

This pass is **not** a replacement for the frozen `git HEAD = 6b50ac7` audit above. It checks the
current dirty working tree after the documented remediation passes and records only newly observed
or still-live mission defects. The prior MAC-/WIN- IDs remain historical; the `CUR-*` IDs below
are the active delta list from this pass.

- **CUR-001** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~385` and
  `Windows/Syxx.Kit/DNSResolver.cs:~248` — `parseResponsePacketDetailed` /
  `ParseResponsePacketDetailed` validates transaction ID and RCODE, but still never requires the
  DNS header QR bit to indicate a response. **Impact:** an on-path injector that can race or forge
  a source-compatible datagram with the expected transaction ID can send a query-form packet carrying
  answer RRs and have Syxx accept it as a resolver response, preserving a spoofing false-clear path
  the roadmap says was closed. **Fix:** reject `flags & 0x8000 == 0` as malformed/non-response and
   add mirrored regression tests.
- **CUR-002** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~117` /
  `Windows/Syxx.Kit/DNSResolver.cs:~137`, paired with `NetworkKeyState.isDNSEncrypted()` /
  `IsDNSEncrypted()` — the public `resolveSecurely` APIs still send plaintext UDP when the system
  resolver list contains loopback, while the typed `encryptedDNSStatus` correctly says loopback
  upstream transport is **unknown**. Current CLIs mostly avoid this API, but it remains public and
  documented as the secure path. **Impact:** any GUI, integrator, or future CLI that calls it can
  report a "secure" resolution through an unverifiable local forwarder or malicious loopback
  resolver. **Fix:** remove/deprecate the boolean secure wrapper or make it return typed
   secure/tampered/inconclusive transport provenance instead of records-only success.
- **CUR-003** [S1] `Windows/Syxx.Kit/VantageComparer.cs:~25` — Windows
  `ResolverQueryOutcome.DidFail` omits `DNSResponseStatus.Truncated`; macOS includes `.truncated`.
  **Impact:** if a local UDP answer is truncated and TCP fallback fails, Windows comparison logic can
  treat that unusable local baseline as a real empty answer and print redirection/censorship instead
  of inconclusive. **Fix:** include `Truncated` in `DidFail` and add a Windows parity regression
  test.
- **CUR-004** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~149` and
  `macOS/Sources/SyxxMirror/SyxxMirror.swift:~67` — macOS comparison output ignores
  `result.isDegraded` and still prints "SECURE" / "SUCCESS" when at least one public vantage point
  failed or returned no usable records. Windows already prints a degraded warning. **Impact:** a
  partial-baseline comparison is over-labeled as clean, creating platform divergence and weaker
  evidence wording on macOS. **Fix:** mirror the Windows degraded wording in both macOS CLIs and
  cover the output path.
- **CUR-005** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~104` — macOS launcher Option A still uses
  the records-only throwing `DNSResolver.queryUDP` path for Step 1, so it loses the typed
  `DNSResponseStatus` that Windows surfaces. **Impact:** NXDOMAIN, NODATA, REFUSED, SERVFAIL, and
  transport failure are collapsed into vague "empty or NXDOMAIN" / "timeout" guidance before the
  user reaches the comparison step. **Fix:** use `queryUDPDetailed` and print the same typed status
  and error detail as Windows.
- **CUR-006** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxRoute/SyxxRoute.swift:~16` and
  `Windows/SyxxRoute/Program.cs:~21` — standalone `syxx-route` still says it is checking route
  shifts/path anomalies, but it only executes traceroute/tracert and echoes hops. **Impact:** users
  are told route anomaly detection occurred when no baseline, ASN, hop-diff, timeout-pattern, or
  path-shift analysis has run. **Fix:** either downgrade the product language to "raw traceroute"
  or implement the structured traceroute/baseline-diff proposal before claiming anomaly detection.

## Data-retention security audit — 2026-07-05 (RET-001…RET-010) [done]

Triggered by a privacy incident (a hardcoded dev shell-prompt string on the public landing page).
Owner asked for a sweep of all three codebases for *"code that stores information but does not
securely erase it after collection."* Three parallel subagent audits + independent verification.
**Structural finding:** before this pass there was **not a single delete/erase call** in either
client (`removeItem`/`SecItemDelete` in macOS, `File.Delete`/`Array.Clear` in Windows) and **no
`DELETE`/TTL/`VACUUM`** anywhere in the server — nothing collected was ever cleaned up. All items
below were remediated in the same pass (both platforms build; macOS 70 / Windows 70 tests pass).

- **RET-001 (S1, HIGH) — Capture files leak the username and never delete.** `syxx-cages`
  (`SyxxCages/SyxxCages.swift`, `SyxxCages/Program.cs`) wrote `DNS Monitor *.txt` NDJSON + report
  to the **current working directory**, world-readable, containing process paths that embed
  `/Users/<name>` / `C:\Users\<name>`. Never deleted. This is the real analog of the website leak.
  **Fixed:** captures now go to an owner-only dir (`~/.syxx/captures` `0700`/`0600`;
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Syxx\captures`), and the raw NDJSON is **erased after the report** unless `--keep`.
- **RET-002 (S1, HIGH) — Passive-DNS ledger is an unbounded, unencrypted browsing history.**
  `Trust/AnswerLedger` persisted domains+resolved IPs+resolvers to `~/.syxx/answer-ledger.json`
  plaintext with no age pruning and no delete path. **Fixed:** 30-day age pruning on load/save,
  `0600` perms (macOS), and a `forget()` API + `syxx-sentinel --forget`.
- **RET-003 (S1, HIGH) — Server retains client IPs forever.** `audit` table (`db.py`) stored raw
  `client_address` IPs on every activate/warp call with no TTL/cap. **Fixed:** `purge_expired()`
  deletes audit rows past `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 7), run on startup + hourly.
- **RET-004 (S1, HIGH) — "One-time" leak token was not one-time; observations outlived tokens.**
  `leak.py verify()` returned observed resolver IPs and deleted nothing; the live DB had orphaned
  observation rows. **Fixed:** `leak_token_consume()` deletes the token + its observations after a
  successful verify; `purge_expired()` also sweeps expired tokens + orphaned observations.
- **RET-005 (S1, HIGH) — `leak_tokens.expires_at` stored but never enforced.** Expired tokens still
  validated; the "expired token" error was dead code. **Fixed:** `leak_token_get()` now rejects
  tokens past `expires_at` on read.
- **RET-006 (S2, HIGH) — `passive_dns` grows unbounded** (count exposed publicly via `/api/stats`).
  **Fixed:** `purge_expired()` prunes rows past `PASSIVE_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 30).
- **RET-007 (S2, MED) — Secrets on the command line.** `syxx-leak --token/--key` and
  `syxx-witness --key` took secrets via argv (visible to `ps`/Task Manager). **Fixed:** env
  fallbacks `SYXX_BEARER_TOKEN` / `SYXX_LICENSE_KEY` / `SYXX_WITNESS_KEY` on both platforms (flags
  still work; env is the recommended path).
- **RET-008 (S2, MED) — Sentinel snapshot persisted plaintext, never deleted.** **Fixed:** `0600`
  perms (macOS) + `forget()` + `syxx-sentinel --forget`.
- **RET-009 (S3, MED) — stale `warp_cache` rows never deleted** (TTL was read-only). **Fixed:**
  `purge_expired()` deletes rows past `WARP_CACHE_TTL`.
- **RET-010 (open, LOW) — in-memory secrets not zeroized.** macOS `String` keys and Windows DPAPI
  transient `byte[]` are left to GC. C# `string` can't be wiped; the Windows `byte[]` buffers can
  (`Array.Clear`) and are **not yet** — tracked as a residual low-severity item.

**Verified-correct-by-design (no change):** license key at rest (Keychain / DPAPI), salted-SHA-256
device fingerprint (never raw), stateless server session tokens (nothing stored), no `%TEMP%`
writes, read-only registry access.

## USER's General Deltas — Syxx-cages [done]

### Syxx-cages not working, Need Revision to Input/Output Format [done]

Syxx-cages needs to be reworked. First, it does not work. No matter what epoch timestamp you add, it
immediately ends its operationn without collecting DNS queries. Secondly, the average user doesn't know what
epoch timestamp notationn means or how to calculate it. So, the app needs to do the heavy lifting for them. We
want users to be able to enter a number of minutes, up to 480 minutes, with the default equaling two minutes. The
app then needs to translate that amount to epoch timestamp notation. Any result, if spun out in epoch timestamp
notation, must then be converted to a normal timestamp on a 12 hour clock.

## Round-1 per-file audit — macOS Deltas (MAC-001…MAC-116)

### SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift

- **MAC-001** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~117` — `parseResponsePacket` ignores RCODE and all header flags, reading only answer count and returning `[]` when 0.
- **MAC-002** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~112` — the response transaction ID is never validated against the query, and the QR bit is never checked.
- **MAC-003** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~86` — `makeQueryPacket` hardcodes transaction ID `0x1234` for every query.
- **MAC-004** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~156` — `sendUDP` accepts the first datagram via `receiveMessage` with no source-address or ID/QR verification.
- **MAC-005** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~118` — the TC (truncation) bit is never checked and there is no TCP fallback; queries are UDP-only.
- **MAC-006** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~200` — `parseName` has no compression-pointer loop guard; pointers may cycle.
- **MAC-007** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~205` — the compression-pointer branch reads `data[current+1]` without bounds-checking.
- **MAC-008** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~185` — `skipName` also lacks a loop guard and second-pointer-byte bounds check.
- **MAC-009** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~120` — the answer loop trusts `answerCount` with only per-record `offset < count` guards; a lying count on a short packet silently `break`s with partial results.
- **MAC-010** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~121` — records are appended for ALL RR types with no filter to the queried type; non-A/AAAA rdata is emitted as raw hex.
- **MAC-011** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~140` — AAAA formatting builds non-canonical IPv6 (no `::` compression) via naive `%x` join.
- **MAC-012** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~40` — `resolveSecurely` trusts `NetworkKeyState.isDNSEncrypted()`; if true it sends plaintext UDP to the default 8.8.8.8 with none of the header/ID validation.
- **MAC-013** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~62` — `queryDoH` sets no request timeout/cancellation; `URLSession.shared` can hang indefinitely.
- **MAC-014** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~64` — DoH treats any non-200 as a generic error and discards the body; RCODE/flags in a 200 dns-message stay unparsed.
- **MAC-015** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~156` — `sendUDP` has no retry, jitter, or multiple probes; a single dropped datagram throws.
- **MAC-016** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~168` — continuation double-resume risk: after an error resumes and cancels, other state transitions or the receive callback can resume again.
- **MAC-017** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~180` — `.waiting(error)` immediately resumes throwing and cancels; transient waiting states are treated as fatal.
- **MAC-018** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~132` — the A-record path requires `rdLength == 4` exactly and otherwise emits hex; no cross-check that RR regions didn't alias into a compression-inflated name.
- **MAC-019** [S3] `DNSResolver.swift:~93` — `makeQueryPacket` silently `continue`s on non-UTF-8 labels and never validates label ≤63 / name ≤255.

### SyxxKit/DNSCapture.swift

- **MAC-020** [S1] `DNSCapture.swift:~205` — `getProcessInfo` fabricates a fake mDNSResponder attribution (path/signingID/pid) whenever `lsof` yields nothing.
- **MAC-021** [S0] `DNSCapture.swift:~232` — `getProcessDetails` fabricates a signingID `com.apple.<name>` regardless of the real code signature.

KDNS-01 | DISAGREE | Success/NODATA is already decided on exact-type answerRecords (CNAME excluded), so a CNAME-only response correctly returns .noData.

## Delta of the Week # 3 (Antigravity) — Conclusion Integrity & End-of-Test Meaning

*Provenance: authored by Antigravity as a peer contribution — **not** a USER directive (retitled
2026-07-06 for accuracy; the USER's own deltas are #1 and #2 in AGENTS.md). The conclusion
vocabulary and CID-001…036 deltas below stand on their merits and were accepted into the combiner.*

Audit date: 2026-07-05. Scope: current dirty working tree, focused only on whether each app's
final conclusion is properly constrained by its own findings. This is distinct from parser,
transport, or feature-completeness deltas: the question here is whether Syxx says the right kind
of thing after the evidence is known.

### Required conclusion vocabulary

Syxx needs a shared conclusion contract before the six checks can be trusted:

- **Untested** — the test was not run, because the user skipped it, the feature was locked, input
  was missing/invalid, privileges were absent, no collector was configured, or a required baseline
  source was not requested. This must never be printed as "inconclusive," "benign," "clear," or
  "secure."
- **Invalidated** — the test began, but a required premise failed: no local resolver, no public
  baseline, local fetch failed, collector receipt absent, raw socket missing for an address family,
  parse failure rate too high, or signature missing. This is stronger than inconclusive: the
  result should not be interpreted.
- **Inconclusive** — the test ran and gathered evidence, but the evidence is insufficient,
  internally inconsistent, or tied between competing interpretations.
- **Degraded** — enough evidence exists for a limited conclusion, but one or more noncritical
  datapoints failed. The conclusion can be shown only with explicit confidence reduction.
- **Positive finding** — tampering/leak/exfiltration/change detected by a probe that actually ran.
- **Negative finding / clean** — allowed only when all required probes for that conclusion ran,
  no invalidator fired, and no positive finding was present.

### Conclusion-influence deltas (CID-001…CID-036) [partial]
>
> **[partial]** — the conclusion vocabulary + synthesis engine + GUI honesty landed (`b911bf9` + GUI
> honesty pass). **Delay:** the per-CLI output-wording subset (Workstream G · LOW priority) is not
> fully swept — the CLIs must never print a conclusion before its premises.

- **CID-001** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~98` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/Syxx/Program.cs:~126` — Prophet falls back to `8.8.8.8` when no system resolver is
  discovered, then presents that as the local DNS server. **Impact:** the actual local-resolver
  test was untested, but the app runs a different public-resolver test and lets subsequent
  findings inherit that substituted premise.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. In `SyxxCLI.swift:98` and `Program.cs:126`, `8.8.8.8` is hardcoded as a fallback. If no system resolver is discovered, a silent public query runs, misrepresenting the local network state.
- **CID-002** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~107` — macOS Prophet uses records-only [Vetting: Agree.]
  `queryUDP` for the A result and infers empty/NXDOMAIN vs timeout from catch state. **Impact:**
  REFUSED, SERVFAIL, NODATA, NXDOMAIN, timeout, and malformed responses cannot properly influence
  the final wording.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. `SyxxCLI.swift:110` calls `DNSResolver.queryUDP` which returns `[DNSRecord]` and swallows the underlying `DNSResponseStatus` in a generic catch block.
- **CID-003** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~128` and [Vetting: Agree.]

- **CID-004** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxNSLook/SyxxNSLook.swift:~73` and [Vetting: Agree.]

  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. The C# witness verification logic checks signature validation matches but fails to print warning flags for inconclusive snapshots.
- **CID-030** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxWitness/SyxxWitness.swift:~46` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/SyxxWitness/Program.cs:~59` — witness creation falls back to `8.8.8.8` when no system
  resolver is detected. **Impact:** the local environment comparison is untested but gets signed
  as if it were the observed resolver context.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. If network config states show no resolvers, `8.8.8.8` is hardcoded as fallback, creating a signed baseline over a mock resolver setup.
- **CID-031** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxSentinel/SyxxSentinel.swift:~31` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/SyxxSentinel/Program.cs:~37` — first Sentinel run says the snapshot is saved as the
  baseline. **Impact:** no comparison has been performed yet, so the result is untested, not
  stable or trustworthy.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. Running Sentinel for the first time outputs configuration saved as stable config, rather than stating that comparisons are untested until a second run occurs.
- **CID-032** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxSentinel/SyxxSentinel.swift:~35` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/SyxxSentinel/Program.cs:~47` — "No change since last run" is printed as stable without
  surfacing whether the captured fields were unknown/boolean-collapsed. **Impact:** unknown DNS
  encryption or VPN state can still produce a reassuring stability conclusion.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. A diff comparison returns stable even if compared states are unknown/unverifiable, masking system degradation.
- **CID-033** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxSentinel/SyxxSentinel.swift:~49` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/SyxxSentinel/Program.cs:~60` — Sentinel rolls the baseline forward after reporting a
  change. **Impact:** an unreviewed suspicious change can become the new normal, allowing the next
  run to say stable.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. Changes are logged and immediately committed, meaning successive runs treat the modification as a stable historical baseline without user approval.
- **CID-034** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI/SyxxCLI.swift:~23` and [Vetting: Agree.]
  `Windows/Syxx/Program.cs:~29` — launcher license status uses boolean validation. **Impact:** a
  network/license-server failure becomes "Lite," and Pro-only tests become untested without a
  precise invalidator.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. Licensing lookup failures result in silent client demotion to Lite, causing Pro tests to exit without showing the invalidating server issue.
- **CID-035** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxApp/AppModel.swift:~118`, `~148`, `~208` — the macOS GUI [Vetting: Agree.]
  repeats the same conclusion leaks: compare can say no tampering when degraded, leak is local-only,
  and warp can overclaim secure. **Impact:** the graphical surface inherits incorrect final
  meanings even when command-line output is improved.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. The GUI controller delegates logic straight to local model booleans and doesn't handle degraded or inconclusive states.
- **CID-036** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxCLI`, `Windows/Syxx`, `SyxxKit`, and `Syxx.Kit` — there is no [Vetting: Agree.]
  shared evidence-to-conclusion contract. **Impact:** every app invents its own terminal wording,
  so fixes land in one command while another still maps untested/invalidated data to inconclusive,
  benign, secure, success, or stable.
  *Evaluation (2026-07-06):* Verified. The lack of an unified evidence-to-verdict contract leads to ad-hoc, disparate terminal wording implementation patterns across the client tools.

### Plan: end-of-test meaning decoder for the six categorical checks

Goal: at the very end of each of the six launcher checks (Prophet, Mirror, Portal, Glutton, Cage,
Witness), Syxx should gather every datapoint produced during that check, validate whether each
required subtest actually ran, and then produce a deterministic interpretation. This is the same
kind of work as the DNS capture interpreter, but applied to cross-discipline datapoints rather
than only captured DNS log rows.

#### 1. Add a shared evidence contract

Implement mirrored Swift/C# types in `SyxxKit` / `Syxx.Kit`:

- `EvidenceExecutionState`: `notRequested`, `untested`, `ran`, `invalidated`, `degraded`,
  `inconclusive`, `positive`, `negative`.
- `EvidencePoint`: stable id, discipline, source tool, value, state, confidence, timestamp,
  human-readable evidence, invalidators, and privacy-redacted raw fields.
- `DisciplineRun`: one run of Prophet/Mirror/Portal/Glutton/Cage/Witness with required evidence
  points, optional evidence points, observed findings, invalidators, and child tool results.
- `MeaningConclusion`: primary conclusion, severity, confidence, candidate alternatives, evidence
  used, evidence not run, invalidators, and next steps.

No final command should print "secure," "benign," "stable," "no leak," or "valid evidence" from
raw booleans. It should print those only from `MeaningConclusion`.

#### 2. Define required datapoints per category

- **Prophet:** system resolver discovery, A and AAAA typed DNS response, DNS header integrity,
  RCODE, DNSSEC status, resolver transport provenance.
- **Mirror:** local resolver outcome, public-vantage quorum, degraded public baseline, content
  local fetch, remote content baseline, script/inline/script-structure comparison.
- **Portal:** resolver list, scoped resolver context, active interfaces, VPN tri-state, captive
  portal tri-state, LAN cartography, route trace, route parse validity.
- **Glutton:** VPN tri-state, system resolver list, collector token, probe dispatch per resolver,
  collector observation, collector receipt/signature, reconciliation status.
- **Cage:** capture privilege, IPv4 socket, IPv6 socket, packet count, parse success rate, process
  attribution confidence, DNS-log/exfil/beacon/blocklist interpretations.
- **Witness:** license validation typed result, network snapshot typed states, Sentinel baseline
  comparison, AnswerLedger drift, witness signature validity, signed evidence quality.

Each required datapoint gets an invalidator rule. Example: `collectorToken.notRequested` means
Glutton is **untested**, not inconclusive; `collectorVerify.ran + no observed resolvers + all probe
dispatches failed` means **invalidated**, not "no leak."

#### 3. Build a deterministic rule engine, not an AI dependency

Use a small offline ruleset that can be represented either as source-coded rules or a bundled
SQLite/JSON table:

- `rules`: id, discipline, conclusion, severity, base score, explanation template.
- `rule_conditions`: rule id, evidence id, operator, expected value/state, weight, required flag.
- `invalidator_precedence`: evidence states that force `untested` or `invalidated` before scoring.
- `next_steps`: conclusion, action text, required capability, privacy note.

Avoid a full Cartesian table of every possible combination; that will explode quickly. A SQL table
is still useful, but it should store predicate rows and weights, not every final state. The engine
can evaluate all matching rules, subtract confidence for degraded/missing optional datapoints, and
select the top conclusion only after invalidators are applied.

#### 4. Reuse the DNS interpreter pattern

`DNSLogAnalyzer` already demonstrates the right model: normalize inputs, count/aggregate
datapoints, then render cautious interpretations. The synthesis engine should reuse that style:

- parse all raw tool outputs into typed `EvidencePoint`s;
- normalize names, IPs, RCODEs, process identities, and timestamps;
- aggregate counts and confidence;
- emit deterministic explanations that name the evidence and the missing evidence.

If the user's Python DNS-capture interpreter has additional heuristics, port them into the same
rules format first for Cage, then generalize them into cross-discipline rules.

#### 5. Integrate at the six check boundaries

Refactor the launcher so each option has a gather phase and a render phase:

1. Gather raw data with no terminal conclusion.
2. Emit raw findings in a "Data observed" section.
3. Pass a `DisciplineRun` to `SyxxMeaningEngine`.
4. Print "Final Meaning" only from the returned `MeaningConclusion`.
5. Set process exit codes from conclusion state (`0` clean, `1` positive finding, `2` degraded or
   inconclusive, `3` untested/invalidated, `4` runtime error).

The standalone tools should use the same engine for their final paragraph. The GUI should display
the same conclusion object, not rephrase booleans independently.

#### 6. Acceptance tests

Add mirrored Swift/C# golden tests for conclusion integrity:

- no system resolver => Prophet/Mirror local resolver is `untested`, never secure;
- public vantage unavailable => Mirror invalidated/inconclusive, never secure;
- one public vantage failed but quorum exists => degraded clean, not secure clean;
- Warp remote baseline unavailable => invalidated, diagnostic rows marked untested;
- Glutton no collector => untested, not inconclusive;
- Glutton all dispatches failed + collector no observations => invalidated, not no leak;
- Cage zero packets => untested/no capture data, not benign;
- high parse-failure capture => invalidated/degraded report;
- Exfil with no timestamps => cadence untested, not benign-by-cadence;
- Witness valid signature over inconclusive comparison => signature valid, evidence inconclusive;
- Sentinel first run => baseline created, comparison untested;
- license validation network error => Pro-gated checks untested due license validation failure.

The rule is simple: no final conclusion may be stronger than its weakest required premise.

## HTTP version issue [vetted]

From the server-based terminal output:

Investigating domain: thisvid.com
· Querying public vantage points…
· IPv4 (A):
  ✓ system: 88.208.57.223
  ✓ 1.1.1.1: 88.208.57.223
  ✓ 8.8.8.8: 88.208.57.223
  ✓ 9.9.9.9: 88.208.57.223
  ✓ cloudflare-doh: 88.208.57.223
  ✓ google-doh: 88.208.57.223
  ✗ quad9-doh: doh http 505
· IPv6 (AAAA):
  ✗ system: system: [Errno -5] No address associated with hostname
  · 1.1.1.1: no records
  · 8.8.8.8: no records
  · 9.9.9.9: no records
  · cloudflare-doh: no records
  · google-doh: no records
  ✗ quad9-doh: doh http 505
Consensus: CONSISTENT-DEGRADED
  reachable vantages agree; some vantages were unreachable
  DNSSEC observed: no (AD bit: unset) — presence-only; not cryptographically validated
you@syxx ~ %

**Interpretation** Clean read overall — here's the breakdown:

- A record consensus. Six of seven vantages answered and all returned the identical single A record, 88.208.57.223. One bare IPv4 with no address spread is characteristic of direct origin hosting rather than an anycast CDN front (Cloudflare/Akamai would show provider ranges, often multiple As). No divergence between your system resolver, plain UDP resolvers, and DoH endpoints means no evidence of hijacking, split-horizon trickery, or local interception rewriting the answer. Notably, your system path returned the same public answer — so NextDNS/Little Snitch's DNS-layer filtering isn't intercepting or sinkholing this domain.
- quad9-doh: HTTP 505. That's "HTTP Version Not Supported" — a transport-layer failure in your DoH client, not a DNS answer. Quad9's endpoint is rejecting the HTTP version your tool negotiated (classic cause: sending HTTP/1.1 request framing to an endpoint expecting HTTP/2, or a malformed version line). This is a tool bug/compat issue worth fixing in LyxDNS rather than a signal about the domain — note it failed identically for both A and AAAA, confirming it's endpoint-level, not query-level.
- IPv6. The domain simply has no AAAA records — every resolver that answered said so. One nit: your system resolver's result is rendered as an error (✗, Errno -5) while the others show a neutral "no records" (·). EAI_NODATA from getaddrinfo is the NODATA case; semantically it's the same outcome and should probably be normalized to ✓/· so the summary line doesn't imply a reachability problem that isn't there.
- Consensus: CONSISTENT-DEGRADED. Correct classification — unanimous agreement among reachable vantages, degraded only because one vantage (quad9-doh) couldn't be queried at all. The distinction between "disagreement" and "missing vantage" is exactly the right thing to preserve.
- DNSSEC. AD bit unset means the zone is (almost certainly) unsigned — no chain of trust from the root. The "presence-only; not cryptographically validated" caveat is the right epistemics: you're reporting what recursive resolvers asserted, not doing your own validation. For an unsigned zone there's nothing to validate anyway, so nothing anomalous, just no cryptographic protection against cache poisoning for this name.

**Verdict:** no red flags in the DNS layer itself — coherent single-origin IPv4 hosting, no v6, unsigned zone, no resolver disagreement. The two actionable items are both on the tooling side: normalize EAI_NODATA to match the "no records" rendering, and debug the HTTP version negotiation against Quad9's DoH endpoint (worth testing whether it works with explicit HTTP/2, since Cloudflare's and Google's endpoints tolerated whatever you sent).

- We need to upgrade the version of HTTP the app defaults to, then apply fallbacks to ensure HTTP versioning errors are caught.

If you disagree with this assessment, please state the basis and propose alternative fixes.

**Peer Vetting & Root-Cause Evaluation (2026-07-07 / Gemini):**

- **Root Cause Verified**: Quad9 deprecated and disabled HTTP/1.1 support for DoH endpoints on December 15, 2025, mandating HTTP/2. Because `Server/syxx_server/resolver.py` queries Quad9 via Python's standard `http.client.HTTPSConnection` (which only supports HTTP/1.1), the server responds with a standard `505 HTTP Version Not Supported` error. Cloudflare and Google DoH endpoints still tolerate HTTP/1.1 fallbacks, which is why they succeeded.
- **Proposed Solution**:
  1. **Server-Side**: Replace `http.client.HTTPSConnection` in `Server/syxx_server/resolver.py` with an HTTP/2-capable client. Since `httpx` supports HTTP/2 out-of-the-box (e.g. `client = httpx.Client(http2=True)`), we can add `httpx[http2]` to the server dependencies and refactor the DoH lookup.
  2. **Fallback**: Catch `505` and socket version errors to mark the vantage status `.degraded` rather than letting the whole query crash or throw a stack trace.
- **Vetting Status**: Agree with the assessment. Recommend adopting option 1 (httpx upgrade) for server-side queries.

This is a supplemental working-tree audit, not an implementation pass. It expands the active delta
inventory to 200 macOS findings and 200 Windows findings so remediation can be triaged at the
call-site level. Several entries are manifestations of a shared root cause; they are still listed
separately where a user-visible command, library boundary, or platform implementation can produce
its own false confidence, missed detection, crash/hang, or weak evidence.

### macOS expanded deltas (MACX-001…MACX-200)

- **MACX-001** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~373` — DNS responses are accepted without requiring the QR bit. **Impact:** forged query-form packets with matching IDs can be parsed as resolver evidence. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-002** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~89` — `DNSResponse.didFail` omits `.truncated`. **Impact:** unusable truncated UDP answers can flow through logic that expects failures to be excluded. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-003** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~116` — `resolveSecurely` sends plaintext UDP when `isDNSEncrypted()` returns true. **Impact:** a public “secure” API can downgrade to unverifiable local UDP. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-004** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~128` — `queryUDP` returns records only. **Impact:** NXDOMAIN, NODATA, REFUSED, SERVFAIL, truncation, and malformed responses are collapsed for legacy callers. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-005** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~180` — `queryDoH` returns records only. **Impact:** HTTPS transport success can mask DNS-layer negative or unusable answers. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-006** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~147` — non-timeout UDP parse/send failures become `.timeout` after retries. **Impact:** hostile malformed packets and network silence are indistinguishable in evidence. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-007** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~197` — DoH accepts any HTTP 200 body as DNS wire data. **Impact:** captive portals or HTML error bodies can be recorded as malformed DNS without HTTP-context attribution. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-008** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~221` — legacy `makeQueryPacket` returns empty data for invalid names. **Impact:** invalid user input can become a zero-length network probe instead of a typed validation failure. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-009** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~392` — TC is reported before RCODE. **Impact:** truncated NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL answers lose their resolver status and become generic truncation. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-010** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~407` — zero-answer responses return `.noData` before question-section validation. **Impact:** malformed replies can be classified as legitimate empty DNS answers. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-011** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~433` — answer parsing breaks on short packets and may return partial success. **Impact:** hostile packets can drop later malformed RRs while preserving earlier “good” answers. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-012** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~489` — CNAME RDATA is hex-encoded rather than decoded as a domain name. **Impact:** CNAME hijacks are hard to compare, report, or classify as blocking answers. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-013** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~579` — invalid UTF-8 labels are silently skipped in `parseName`. **Impact:** malformed or evasive owner names can be normalized into misleading evidence. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-014** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~622` — NWConnection `.waiting` is treated as terminal failure. **Impact:** transient interface changes can become false resolver failures. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-015** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~689` — TCP fallback reuses the short UDP timeout. **Impact:** degraded networks can turn truncation recovery into an inconclusive or failed probe. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-016** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~713` — TCP DNS length prefixes are accepted without a tighter DNS message-size policy. **Impact:** hostile peers can force oversized allocations within the 16-bit DNS envelope. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-017** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~751` — `recordsOrThrow` returns empty arrays for negative DNS statuses. **Impact:** callers can confuse “domain does not exist” with “query succeeded with no notable evidence.” [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-018** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~373` — response question name/type are not enforced as the queried tuple. **Impact:** same-ID cross-answer races can pollute comparisons. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-019** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~421` — returned answer RRs are not filtered to the requested owner. **Impact:** extra or unrelated answers can influence downstream verdicts. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-020** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~128` — UDP queries do not request EDNS buffer sizing. **Impact:** large DNSSEC or modern record sets are more likely to truncate and degrade comparisons. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-021** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~197` — DoH requests do not set an explicit `Accept: application/dns-message`. **Impact:** proxy or server content negotiation failures are harder to diagnose. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-022** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~221` — query construction lacks IDNA failure provenance. **Impact:** internationalized-domain validation errors can be flattened into generic malformed input. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-023** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~489` — NS, PTR, MX, SOA, SRV, and TXT-like RDATA are not semantically decoded. **Impact:** evidence reports cannot explain many tampering-relevant record changes. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-024** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~147` — retry logic has no resolver rotation metadata. **Impact:** users cannot tell whether multiple attempts hit the same failing resolver path. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-025** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift:~116` — the public secure-resolution path returns no transport provenance. **Impact:** signed or displayed results cannot prove whether UDP, TCP, or DoH produced the answer. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-026** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSSECVerifier.swift:~68` — the boolean DNSSEC API returns true for expired/not-yet-valid signatures. **Impact:** stale or future-dated DNSSEC material can be reported as verified. [Vetting: Agree.]

- **MACX-030** [S0] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSSECVerifier.swift:~78` — parent DS-chain validation is absent. **Impact:** trust is not anchored to the DNSSEC hierarchy. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-031** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSSECVerifier.swift:~94` — RRSIG windows are not tied to the RRset/type being evaluated. **Impact:** signatures for another type can influence the verdict. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-032** [S1] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSSECVerifier.swift:~94` — unparsable RRSIG timing falls back to “records present unverified.” **Impact:** malformed signatures get softened instead of flagged as broken evidence. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MACX-033** [S2] `macOS/Sources/SyxxKit/DNSSECVerifier.swift:~112` — DNSSEC time comparison ignores serial-number edge cases. **Impact:** rollover-adjacent validity windows can be misclassified. [Vetting: Agree.]

## Little Snitch "modified" error after privilege escalation

- Immediately after entering Users' password at app launch, Little Snitch throws out an error stating:
**The program “syxx” has been modified
Previously, the program was only ad-hoc signed. For later identity checks a checksum of the program was stored. This checksum does not match anymore. This probably means that the program was updated meanwhile. However, it’s also possible that the program has been replaced by malware.**
- Issue is obviously related to User's signature status. It's unclear why the app is saying that User's signature changed, however.
- No fixes to suggest.

**Peer Vetting & Root-Cause Evaluation (2026-07-07 / Gemini):**

- **Root Cause Verified**: Little Snitch uses macOS Designated Requirements (DR) to identify applications. For ad-hoc signed apps (like standard local developer builds of `syxx`), there is no stable anchor to an Apple Developer ID team. Thus, Little Snitch stores a raw cryptographic checksum of the binary. Every rebuild of the app during development modifies the binary's checksum, prompting Little Snitch to warn that the program has been modified.
- **Proposed Solution**:
  1. **Development Workaround**: Add a self-signed or local certificate to sign the app stably during development, or add the local binary to Little Snitch's exception rules.
  2. **Production Fix (Notarization)**: Once Developer ID certificates are active and the app is officially signed and notarized (as slated for this week), the binary will have a stable, Apple-anchored DR (`anchor apple generic and identifier "app.syxx" and ...`). Little Snitch will verify the developer signature chain rather than raw checksums, resolving the warning permanently.
  3. **Escalation Hardening**: Avoid running raw escalated scripts inline. Move privileged operations (such as capture socket creation in `syxx-cages`) to a dedicated, signed helper tool using `SMJobBless` or `ServiceManagement` APIs.
- **Vetting Status**: Agree with the assessment. This is expected behavior for local ad-hoc developer builds and is fully resolved by the upcoming Developer ID signing/notarization pipeline.

## SyxxKit/DNSResolver.swift

- **MAC-001** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~117` — `parseResponsePacket` ignores RCODE and all header flags, reading only answer count and returning `[]` when 0. **Impact:** a spoofed/censored NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty answer; the core hijack signal is discarded. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-002** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~112` — the response transaction ID is never validated against the query, and the QR bit is never checked. **Impact:** off-path spoofed/injected UDP replies (classic cache poisoning) are accepted as authoritative, yielding a false "resolved" verdict. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-003** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~86` — `makeQueryPacket` hardcodes transaction ID `0x1234` for every query. **Impact:** a predictable XID makes response spoofing trivial and correlation impossible, defeating injection detection. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-004** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~156` — `sendUDP` accepts the first datagram via `receiveMessage` with no source-address or ID/QR verification. **Impact:** an on-path injector that wins the race is returned as truth, a false negative. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-005** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~118` — the TC (truncation) bit is never checked and there is no TCP fallback; queries are UDP-only. **Impact:** truncated (or deliberately truncated) responses silently return partial/empty answers read as "no records." [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-006** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~200` — `parseName` has no compression-pointer loop guard; pointers may cycle. **Impact:** a malformed/malicious response with a self-referential pointer hangs the parser, denying analysis on hostile input. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-007** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~205` — the compression-pointer branch reads `data[current+1]` without bounds-checking. **Impact:** a packet truncated on a pointer's first byte crashes the scan (OOB index), aborting detection. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-008** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~185` — `skipName` also lacks a loop guard and second-pointer-byte bounds check. **Impact:** malformed question-section compression corrupts the answer offset so real answers are missed or misread. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-009** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~120` — the answer loop trusts `answerCount` with only per-record `offset < count` guards; a lying count on a short packet silently `break`s with partial results. **Impact:** forged/truncated packets produce a partial set treated as a valid result. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-010** [S1] `DNSResolver.swift:~121` — records are appended for ALL RR types with no filter to the queried type; non-A/AAAA rdata is emitted as raw hex. **Impact:** CNAME/other RRs pollute the answer set so downstream comparison compares hex blobs/unrelated records. [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-011** [S2] `DNSResolver.swift:~140` — AAAA formatting builds non-canonical IPv6 (no `::` compression) via naive `%x` join. **Impact:** the same IPv6 answer renders differently from reference resolvers, causing spurious mismatches (false positives). [Vetting: Agree.]
- **MAC-012** [S0] `DNSResolver.swift:~40` — `resolveSecurely` trusts `NetworkKeyState.isDNSEncrypted()`; if true it sends plaintext UDP to the default 8.8.8.8 with none of the header/ID validation. **Impact:** on a MITM'd network reporting "encrypted," it falls back to unauthenticated UDP and reports the attacker's answer as secure. [Vetting: Agree with clarification. The fix should treat loopback forwarders as unknown transport, not as encrypted.]
